newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russian regions edge on to Eurobond market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russian regions edge on to Eurobond market.

text.p: Russia's Komi Republic, which said last month it was working on an international credit rating, might not seem an obvious candidate to tap foreign capital markets for funds.

A sparsely-populated former penal colony in northwestern Russia stretching past the Arctic circle, Komi has just 1.2 million people inhabiting 416,000 square km (161,000 square miles) of dense fir and birch forests.
Like many of the 89 regions that make up the vast Russian Federation, it rarely enters Russia's political spotlight.
But that is no obstacle to issuing a Eurobond in the minds of some Komi officials.
They view recent successful issues by Moscow and Russia's second city St Petersburg, and reform crusader Nizhny Novgorod's forthcoming launch, as a sign of how successful Komi's could be.

"We supply St Petersburg with oil and coal. I mean it just as an example -- why can they do it, and we can't? I consider that we have enough reason (to do it)," said Komi Finance Minister Alexander Zakharov.
This approach is clearly representative of a long list of far-flung regions, desperate for cheap credit, that have announced Eurobond plans in past months.
STRUGGLING REGIONS SEEK INVESTMENT AND CHEAP CREDIT

Russia's headlong economic reforms have left many regions, often heavily, if not exclusively, dependent on a single industry, reeling under the burden of spiralling production and a web of debt between companies and government.

Huge delays in wage and pension payments and strikes in some sectors have led many regional governors to condemn the federal government's strict monetary policies and complain that Moscow is insensitive to regional problems.

But some, inspired by the example of the central government, which only recently placed a third, $2 billion issue, see a Eurobond as an extension of efforts to attract foreign investment for structural reforms and production projects.
Viktor Veltsovsky, head of Komi's department of foreign and regional relations, said Western investment was $59 million in 1996, up 60 percent from 1995. He forecast $100 million in 1997.
He said the figure included a German credit deal backed by exports to finance various oil and wood processing projects.
"For us the ideal situation would be when we could attract a billion dollars a year -- but there's a big difference between $100 million and $1 billion," he said.
But while the list is as varied as it is long, the chances of the majority of Eurobond hopefuls tapping international markets remains unclear.
RUSSIA WARY OF REGIONAL PROBLEMS

Some regions, like the autonomous Tatarstan republic, have scaled back plans with the approach of initial bold deadlines, while others, like the southern Mary El republic, have dropped them altogether, unsure of their ability to guarantee the loans.
More importantly, the federal government, wary of being lumbered with bad regional debt later, has adopted a cautious approach to regional administrations.

Moscow, St Petersburg and Nizhny Novgorod received permission to issue bonds only following a presidential decree, and appeared to have been chosen as Russia's three most economically stable and forward-looking cities.
Meanwhile, a draft law on regional Eurobonds says regions receiving funding from the federal government cannot issue Eurobonds, a clause the Finance Ministry said in April applied to Komi.
Moscow could have reason to be cautious. Komi suffers from the same economic problems as many of Russia's other, less well-endowed regions.

Teachers, doctors and city employees, all of them on the regional or city administration payroll, say they have not been paid for months, while many of the region's big industrial enterprises owe billions of roubles in back taxes.
The picture is much the same in the other regions.
Moscow's hesitant approach was glossed over by Zakharov, who says Komi sends 44 percent of revenue to central state coffers.
But Deputy Economics Minister Sergei Frolov, part of a Komi team working on getting an international credit rating, made clear the regions had heard and understood Moscow's message.
He said any eventual Eurobond placement, as well as its size and maturity, would depend on talks with Moscow, the rating and market conditions.
REGIONS FORGE AHEAD WHERE MOSCOW FEARS TO TREAD

The race to issue cheap credit has also prompted warnings that the market will be swamped, but in Komi, as in the Sverdlovsk, Samara, Irkutsk and Perm regions and the republic of Sakha, preparations are quietly continuing.
Officials say Komi's natural wealth -- it is rich in oil, coal and timber -- makes it as likely a Eurobond candidate as any.
"I think that Western entrepreneurs are very interested in Komi Republic as a region for raw materials, where they can put money in and get a payback," said Zakharov.

Untapped until Soviet dictator Josef Stalin's repression sent thousands of prisoners to forced labour camps in the 1930s and 1940s, Komi's wealth of natural resources is now drawing foreign investors hungry for profits.

Since the start of Russian economic reforms, Western firms such as the former British Gas, which split into BG Plc and Centrica in February, and Swiss Glencore International AG have rushed to form joint ventures with local oil company Komineft and its recently-formed parent company KomiTEK.

And with more lining up to begin work on oil fields in Komi's far north once a delayed production-sharing agreement comes into effect, the republic's officials appear to have good evidence of what they say is an investment-friendly zone.
For Zakharov, unlocking Komi's hidden wealth is the key to a brighter future.
"The republic is one of the leading economic regions of Russia," he said. "The economic potential is here, the raw materials are here."
